summary.title: Continuous Integration
summary.one_liner: Continuous Integration means every developer merges work into a shared mainline at least daily, with each integration verified by an automated build and test suite so errors surface quickly.
takeaways: Integrate work into a single shared mainline at least once a day, verifying each integration with an automated build including tests.
Keep everything needed to build and run the product in version control, and store build instructions as text so changes can be diffed.
Automate the build with a dependency-network tool and make the build self-testing so any failing test fails the build.
Fix broken builds immediately and keep the build fast so integration stays cheap and frequent.
summary.summary: Martin Fowler's article defines Continuous Integration as a practice where team members merge changes into a shared mainline at least daily, with each merge checked by an automated build and tests. It explains the problems of long-running feature branches and late integration, then walks through a worked example of adding a feature with frequent pulls, local builds, and CI service verification. The article then covers core practices: a version-controlled mainline, full automation of builds, self-testing code (with TDD as a common route), frequent commits to mainline, and related topics such as deployment and common questions. It is a conceptual guide with practical rules rather than a hands-on tutorial.
